newsitem.title: CHINA: China record state debt expected to sell smoothly.
newsitem.headline: China record state debt expected to sell smoothly.

text.p: China's record issue of state debt for 1997 is expected to sell smoothly, mainly due to continued strong growth in personal bank deposits and new incentives to boost sales, analysts said on Thursday.

The issue is also likely to push up state debt prices on the secondary market due to the lower yields of the new debt with inflation falling and the central bank expected to cut bank interests rates again this year, they said.
China's target for domestic and overseas debt in 1997 is 248.596 billion yuan ($29.95 billion), an increase of 27.3 percent over 1996, the Finance Ministry said early this month.
The ministry did not give a breakdown for the issue, but in the past few years, more than 95 percent of China's state debt has been sold domestically.

"Despite the huge amount, sales will be smooth with individual bank deposits surging," said an Shanghai-based banker. "The stock markets are too risky and other investment channels are few. That pushes investors to buy the debt."
"The central government has already taken some measures to ensure a smooth issue," said a state debt trader with China Guotai Securities.

The Finance Ministry last month announced 10 new measures to make it more convenient for retail investors to trade state debt by opening more sales outlets and allowing investors to open special state debt trading accounts.
Analysts said sales would be helped by Beijing's decision to set coupon rates for this year's issue higher than those for bank deposits.

For a recent batch of 123 billion yuan non-tradable treasury notes of two, three and five years starting March 1, Beijing has set the annual coupons at about one percentage point higher than interest rates for bank deposits of the same duration.
China bank deposits grew sharply again last year, albeit more slowly than in 1995, due to two interest rate cuts by the central bank in May and August 1996.

New bank deposits in China from January to November in 1996 totalled 820.19 billion yuan, up 12 percent year-on-year. Total private savings amounted to 3,791.73 billion yuan at the end of November, official figures show.
Analysts said they expected the central bank to cut bank interest rates again in 1997 with inflation falling to a year-on-year 6.1 percent for 1996 from a year-on-year 14.8 percent in 1995.
Traders said the yields of the existing spot state debt contracts on the secondary market were much higher despite the high coupons set for the latest batch of treasury notes.
Beijing had allowed high interest rates for bank deposits and state debt issues in the past few years because of high inflation rates, giving the contracts very high returns.
The higher yields of the existing contracts against the new state debt has pushed up the prices of the contracts on the open market over the past few weeks, traders said.

"Institutions will surely further push up the prices of existing contracts on the secondary market," said a trader with Fujian Industrial Securities. Individuals in China rarely trade on the spot secondary market.
The Finance Ministry has said China will issue 57 billion yuan to cover the budget deficit in 1997 while a further 195.908 billion yuan would be needed to service domestic and foreign debt.
That gives a total of 252.908 billion yuan, but a surplus of 4.312 billion yuan from bond receipts in 1996 will be deducted.
China issued 196.742 billion yuan in state debt last year, or 1.485 billion yuan above the budgeted figure of 195.257 billion yuan.
